chapter.simpara: The vision document is the product team's primary deliverable. It establishes the shared understanding of the product across all stakeholders and teams and serves as the authoritative reference for the product's direction throughout the project lifecycle.

listitem.simpara: What. What the product is and does.
Why. The problem it addresses and why it matters.
Who. The stakeholder groups it serves and the value it delivers to each.
How. The lifecycle phases through which the product will be built and delivered.
Success. The key success indicators and the metrics used to observe them.

section.title: Applicable standards
section.simpara: No known standard specifically governs product vision documents.

section.title: Ownership
section.simpara: The vision document is owned by the product team and authored by the product lead.

section.title: Structure
section.simpara: The document is structured as follows:

listitem.simpara: Introduction. Product and environment overview; purpose and scope of the document; applied playbooks.
Purpose. The problem the product addresses and the motivation for building it.
Stakeholders and value propositions. One subsection per stakeholder group, each describing the group's core needs and the value propositions that address them.
Lifecycle. The named phases of the project lifecycle, their goals, and the gates between them.
Key success indicators. The KSIs, the metrics used to observe them at each lifecycle phase, and a summary table mapping value propositions to KSIs.
Getting involved. How external contributors and stakeholders can participate in the project.
Feedback. How readers can submit feedback on the document.
Glossary. Terms introduced or used in the document.
Bibliography. External documents referenced in the text.

section.title: Maintenance
section.simpara: The vision document is reviewed and updated whenever the product's direction changes significantly — for example, when a new stakeholder group is identified, a value proposition is retired, or the lifecycle is restructured. Routine updates to metrics and thresholds do not require a full review cycle. Each revision must be reflected in the document's revhistory.

The sections most likely to evolve are Stakeholders and value propositions, as market and community feedback accumulates, and Key success indicators, as early metrics are replaced by stronger signals. The Purpose and Lifecycle sections are more stable and should change only when the fundamental rationale or structure of the project shifts.
